transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, it’s... it's a bit of a long story, to be honest with you. I’m an operations manager over at the plant—been working my way up there since I was just a kid, really, since I didn't have much schooling to fall back on. I'm used to handling problems, fixing things, keeping the whole floor moving. But lately... well, I came in today because I just keep having these thoughts, and I can't seem to shake them no matter how hard I try to keep my mind busy. 

It’s mostly at night, or when I’m driving in to work before the sun even comes up. I just sit there and keep thinking that my family—my wife, the kids, even though they're older now—that they might actually just be better off if I didn't wake up in the morning. Like it would just be easier for everybody if I just wasn't around anymore. And it’s not just a passing thing, it’s this heavy, constant drum in my head. 

It got so bad the other morning, I was sitting in my truck in the lot at work, just staring at the steering wheel, and it actually scared the living daylights out of me. I realized how real it was starting to feel. So I went inside and I actually told my supervisor about it. I've known the guy for twenty years, and I just broke down and said, "I'm having these thoughts about not waking up." And that scared me enough to finally listen to him when he told me I had to leave shift and come see somebody like you. Because it’s just not right, you know? A man shouldn't be thinking about how his family would do better with him gone. I just... I don't know how it got to this point, but I can't keep going on like this.
Have you been enjoying the things you usually like to do lately?

Well, doc... that’s the thing, I just... I don't know what happened to me. I used to be a guy who always had something going on, always had a project or something to look forward to. Like, out back, I have these raised beds I built a few years ago. I used to spend hours out there, messing with my tomato plants. I’d be out there pulling weeds, checking the soil, tying up the vines... I was real particular about my tomatoes. And if I wasn't doing that, I'd be in the garage. I have a little workbench set up where I’d just sand wood, you know? Not even making anything fancy, just sanding down old pieces of oak or pine, getting them smooth. It was quiet, gave me something to do with my hands. 

And on Sundays, man, Sundays used to be my favorite. I’d go to church with the wife, and afterwards, I’d be the guy staying late, standing out in the parking lot or the vestibule, just shooting the breeze with the other guys for an hour. And then I'd come home, get in my recliner, and watch the Falcons game. I never missed a game. Even when they were having a rough season, I’d be right there yelling at the TV. 

But lately... I don't know. I walk past the garden and the weeds are taking over, and I just look at it. I look at the tomatoes rotting on the vine, and I don't even care. I walk into the garage and see my workbench, and it just... it feels like it belongs to somebody else. Like some other guy used to stand there and sand wood. I haven't turned on a football game in weeks. And church... I still go because my wife wants me to, but the minute the service is over, I just make a beeline for the truck. I don't want to talk to anybody. I don't want to stand around. I just want to go home and sit in the quiet. It’s like all the color just got washed out of everything I used to like doing.
Have you been feeling pleasure or enjoyment from anything at all lately?

Honestly, doc, like I was just saying... it's just nothing. Zero. I know I just went on a whole tear about the tomato plants, and sanding wood at my bench, and watching the Falcons, and staying after church to talk with the guys... but to answer you straight, no. No pleasure from anything at all. 

I even try to force it, I really do. I'll sit down in my recliner and think, "Okay, I'm gonna watch this game and I'm gonna enjoy it," but I just stare at the screen and feel completely empty. I look at all that stuff—my tools, my garden, my Sunday routine—and like I said, it really does just feel like it belongs to somebody else. Like I'm a ghost walking around in my own house looking at some other man's life. 

I don't get a kick out of a good meal anymore. My wife made my favorite chicken fried steak the other night and I chewed it like it was cardboard. I don't care about a hot cup of coffee in the morning, I don't even crack a smile when one of the guys on the floor tells a joke. It's just this big, heavy blankness all the time. So, no, I can't think of a single thing that brings me any joy right now. It's like the part of me that feels good about things just packed up and walked off the job.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, doc, if I had to put a pin in it... I've been trying to figure that out myself, tracing it back, you know? Because a man wants to know why his engine's stalling out. And it seems like this whole... this whole change in me, it’s been going on for right about two weeks now. 

It started right exactly when my youngest—my daughter—she packed up and left Georgia. She joined up with the military. Army, actually. She's always been a tough kid, always wanted to do something big with her life, which I'm proud of, I really am. But man, when the day actually came... we drove her down to the processing station, and I hugged her goodbye, and it just hit me like a ton of bricks. I remember driving back home with my wife, and the truck was just so dead quiet. Usually, we'd have the country station on, or we'd be talking about what we needed to pick up from the grocery store, but I just couldn't say a single word. 

And ever since that day—which was exactly two weeks ago this past Tuesday—it's like somebody just pulled the plug on me. I thought at first I was just sad to see her go, you know how it is. Any father would be. You raise 'em to leave the nest, you want them to go out and make a life, but it still aches when they finally fly. But it didn't get better. Day three, day four, week one, week two... the house just feels huge and empty now, even with the wife there, and this heavy feeling just kept settling in deeper and deeper. So yeah, it’s been two weeks. Two solid weeks since she shipped out that I've been stuck like this.
Have you had any thoughts of actually acting on these feelings of not waking up, or of harming yourself in any way?

Well, doc... that’s... that’s the real reason I’m sitting in this chair right now. Because, see, it started out as just this heavy feeling, like I said, just feeling like everything was gray and empty after my girl left. But then... then it started getting darker. 

I’d be lying in bed at night, staring up at the ceiling fan going round and round, and my wife would be asleep next to me, and I’d just think... "What if I just didn't wake up?" And at first, it was just a passing thought, you know? Like, "Man, it would be so much easier to just sleep through all this." But then it started sticking. It started playing on a loop in my head. I'd be driving to work, looking at the road, and the thought would just pop up: "They'd probably be better off. My wife wouldn't have to deal with me moping around like a ghost. My daughter’s off starting her life, she doesn't need a dad who can't even get out of his recliner." 

It got to the point where it wasn't just a thought anymore, it felt like... like this awful, heavy truth that I couldn't shake. And it scared me. It really scared me, doc. I’ve always been the provider, the guy who takes care of things, and suddenly my own brain is telling me the best way to take care of them is to just... not be here. 

I didn't tell my wife. I couldn't. But I was at work, sitting in my office at the plant, and I just... I broke down. I don't cry. I'm a 57-year-old manager, I don't sit at my desk and cry. But I did. And my supervisor, Jim—good guy, known him for fifteen years—he walked in and saw me. He sat me down, closed the door, and I just spilled it. I told him about the thoughts. I told him how scared I was that I was starting to believe them. And he was the one who told me I needed to come in here. He said, "You can't mess around with that kind of thinking, you gotta talk to somebody." So... no, I haven't made a plan or tried to do anything, but the thoughts... yeah, they're there. And they're exactly why I came in.
Have you lost any weight recently?

Well, doc, since you ask... yeah, I suppose I have. I haven't exactly been stepping on the scale or anything, because like I said, I just don't care enough to do it. But my belt... my work belt, the leather one I've worn every day to the plant for the last five years, it's definitely sitting looser. I had to pull it to the next notch just the other morning, and even then my work pants felt like they were sagging. My wife noticed it too. She was doing the laundry and she held up a pair of my jeans and said, "These are going to fall right off you." 

And it makes sense, really, because I just... I have zero appetite. Like I was saying before about that chicken fried steak... food just doesn't appeal to me anymore. Most days, I have to literally force myself to take a few bites just so my stomach stops rumbling, but even that feels like a chore. It's like chewing on sawdust. I'll take my lunch pail to the warehouse—my wife always packs me a good lunch, usually a turkey sandwich on that thick bread I used to love, maybe some potato salad or an apple—and I'll sit there in the breakroom with the guys, and I just look at it. I'll take it out of the Tupperware, maybe take one bite, and then it just sits there. I end up wrapping it back up or just throwing it right in the trash before I go back on the floor. 

It's the same thing at home. We'll sit down for dinner, and she'll have made a pot roast or spaghetti, stuff I'd normally go back for seconds on, and I just push it around my plate with my fork. I try to eat a little so she doesn't get upset, because she works hard on those meals, but I just can't stomach it. It's like my whole system is just shut down. I don't feel hungry, I don't crave anything, I don't look forward to eating. So yeah, I'm definitely dropping weight, just because I can't bring myself to put anything in my mouth most of the time.
Have you been feeling slowed down or restless lately?

Slowed down? Yeah, doc, that's... that's exactly it. It's funny you use those words, because just the other day, I was trying to explain it to my wife and I just couldn't find the right way to say it. But "slowed down" is putting it mildly. It's more like... well, it feels like my whole body is just moving through mud. Thick, heavy mud, right up to my waist. 

You know, I've been managing the floor at the plant for a long time, and usually, I'm the guy pacing up and down, checking the lines, talking to the foremen, always on the move. I've always had a lot of hustle. But these last couple of weeks? I can barely drag myself from my office to the loading dock. It takes me twice as long just to walk across the warehouse floor. I'm just shuffling along. And it's not just the walking, either, it's... it's my head, too. Like my brain is in that same mud. 

Just yesterday, one of my guys, Tommy—he runs the forklift on the day shift—he came up to me asking a real simple question about the shipping schedule. Something I know like the back of my hand, something I've answered a thousand times. And I just stood there. I was looking right at him, and I heard him, but it took me forever to actually process what he said and get the words out to answer him. I just stared at him blankly for what felt like a whole minute before I could spit out a basic answer. It's embarrassing, honestly. 

And the guys at work, they're definitely noticing. People keep pulling me aside, asking if I'm coming down with something, asking if I'm sick or if I need to go home and sleep off a bug. Because they see it. They see me moving so slow, taking forever to answer simple questions, just not being the guy who usually runs the show. I just feel so heavy all the time, doc. Like gravity got turned up to double on me. So no, I wouldn't say restless at all. Just... bogged down. Completely stuck in the mud.
Have you been experiencing these feelings of sadness and emptiness every day since your daughter left?

Yeah, doc, every single day. It’s... well, it’s been about two weeks now. Two weeks since she packed up and left Georgia for the military. And I mean every single day since then, it’s just been this... this heavy, dark cloud sitting right on my chest. 

I remember the morning she left like it was yesterday, but honestly, it also feels like a lifetime ago because these last couple weeks have just dragged on so much. We were standing out in the driveway, right there in front of the house we've lived in for twenty years. The sun was just coming up, kind of casting that orange light over everything, and she had her duffel bags all stuffed in the trunk of her little Honda. I helped her check the oil and the tire pressure one last time, because, you know, that's what a dad does, you gotta make sure the car is safe for a long trip. And then she hugged me, and she hugged her mom, and she got in and drove off to start basic training. 

And ever since those taillights disappeared down the street... man, it's just been this constant emptiness. Two whole weeks of it. I wake up, and for a split second, I forget she's gone, but then it hits me all over again. And it's not just missing her, you know? It's natural to miss your kid when they leave the nest, I know that. But it's like all the color just drained right out of the world the minute she crossed the state line. Two whole weeks of just... nothing. Just waking up and feeling completely hollowed out, day in and day out, without a single break. I keep thinking maybe tomorrow I'll wake up and feel like my old self, the guy who gets things done, but nope. Every day, same gray emptiness, from the minute I open my eyes till I'm staring at that ceiling fan at night.
Have your feelings of sadness and emptiness lasted for most of the day, every day, for the past two weeks?

Yeah, doc, most of the day. Honestly, pretty much the whole day, from the second I open my eyes. But... you know, I was sitting in my recliner the other night, just staring at the TV without really watching it, and I started really thinking about it. And... well, looking back on it now, it hasn't just been these past two weeks. 

I mean, the two weeks since she left, that's definitely been the most intense, the heaviest it's been, without a doubt. But these low stretches... they’ve actually been coming around for about a year now. I just didn't really want to admit it to myself, I guess. I'd have these periods over the last twelve months where I'd just feel that same kind of gray feeling creeping in. I'd be at the plant, looking out over the floor, and I'd just feel totally drained and hollow for a while. I kept telling myself it was just the stress of the job, or maybe I was just getting older and not bouncing back like I used to. Because, you know, when you're managing operations, you don't really have time to sit around feeling sorry for yourself. You just push through. 

So I'd push through, and maybe it would lift a little, but then another low stretch would come rolling back in a few months later. It’s been happening like that for a solid year. It's just that... this one, this particular stretch right now after my daughter left, it has hit me the absolute hardest by a long shot. It's like all those other times over the past year were just a warm-up, because this one knocked the wind completely out of me, and it just sits there all day, every day, making it impossible to ignore like I used to.
Have you felt sad or empty for at least two weeks straight since your daughter left?

Well, yeah, doc, that's... that's exactly what I've been trying to say. It's been a solid two weeks of this. Two straight weeks since she pulled out of the driveway and headed off for basic training. 

I remember looking at the calendar that morning, you know, marking the day she left because it was such a big deal for us, for the whole family. And I haven't been able to shake this feeling since that very morning. Not for a single day. It's like a switch flipped the minute her car turned the corner at the end of our street. I thought maybe I'd just need a couple of days to adjust, you know, get used to the house being quieter, get used to not seeing her shoes by the front door or hearing her playing her music in her room. But it hasn't let up at all. 

Every single day for the last fourteen days, I wake up and there's that same heavy, empty feeling right in my gut. It's been two weeks of dragging myself through the motions, feeling like I'm just hollowed out inside. So, yeah, to answer your question, it's been exactly two weeks straight of feeling this way, ever since she left Georgia for the military. I just can't seem to shake it, no matter what I do.
Have you felt this low almost every day since your daughter left, without any days where you felt significantly better?

I feel like I’m beating a dead horse here, doc, but yes, sir. Like I’ve been saying, this whole change in me has been going on for about two weeks since my daughter left Georgia for the military, and there hasn't been a single break in it. Not one. 

You’d think maybe I’d get a breather, right? Like maybe on a Saturday, when I don't have to go down to the plant and deal with the operations and the floor supervisors, I might wake up and think, 'Hey, maybe today won't be so bad.' My wife even tried to get me out of the house last Sunday, just to take a drive down by the river, the way we used to when the kids were little. Bless her heart, she was really trying to cheer me up, talking about the trees and the weather and trying to get my mind off things, but I just sat there in the truck. I couldn't even force a smile for her. 

So no, there hasn't been a single day where I felt significantly better. It's just been this heavy, flat line of feeling low, every single day for this whole two-week stretch since she shipped out. I keep waiting for the clouds to part, you know? Just one afternoon where I feel like my old self, the guy who can handle whatever life throws at him, but it just hasn't happened. Not a single good day in these past two weeks.
Have you felt this low for most of every day since your daughter left, without any letup?

Doc, I gotta ask... is my microphone working? Because I feel like I'm just repeating myself over and over here. Yes, sir. Like I've been trying to tell you, this whole change in me has been going on for about two weeks now, right since my daughter left Georgia for the military. 

And when I say without any letup, I mean *zero* letup. Most of the day, every single day. I honestly don't know how many different ways I can explain it to you. It's not like it comes and goes, or like I get a couple hours in the afternoon where I feel fine. It's just sitting there, heavy, from the minute I wake up and pour my coffee till the minute I try to go to sleep. Two weeks. Fourteen days. 

I know you got your clipboard and your specific questions you gotta get through, and I respect that, I really do—like I said, I manage folks at the plant, I know how standard operating procedures work and why you gotta check all the boxes. But I promise you, if there was a day or even a few hours where I felt like my old self again, I'd be the first to tell you. I'd be thrilled to tell you. But there just hasn't been. It's like a thick fog rolled in the second she crossed the state line, and it just hasn't burned off. So, yes, two weeks straight. Every day. Most of the day. No letup at all.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities you usually enjoy for more than half of the days since your daughter left?

Well, doc, that's... yeah. That’s a big part of it, actually. And when you say "more than half the days," I gotta be honest, it's every single day. 

My wife was just getting on me about the yard the other day. I usually... well, I used to love messing with my tomato plants. I got this little patch out back, raised beds I built myself a few years ago, and usually by this time of year I'm out there every evening. I'd be checking the soil, pulling weeds, tying up the vines so they don't snap under the weight. I took pride in it. But lately? I look out the kitchen window at 'em and it's just... I don't know, it's like looking at a neighbor's yard. Like it belongs to somebody else entirely. 

Same goes for my workbench out in the garage. I usually spend hours out there just sanding wood, working on little projects, making birdhouses or fixing up old chairs for folks. The smell of the sawdust, the feel of the grain smoothing out under my hands... it used to settle my mind after a long shift at the plant. Now, the tools are just gathering dust. I walk right past the bench and don't even care to flick the light on. 

And it ain't just the chores or the hobbies, either. Sundays... Sundays used to be my favorite day of the week. We'd go to church, and I was always the guy staying after, drinking that terrible percolator coffee in the fellowship hall, just talking everybody's ear off about how their week went. Then I'd come home, settle into my recliner, and watch the Falcons play. I've been a Falcons fan my whole life, through all the heartbreak, you know? But the last couple of Sundays since my girl left? I didn't even care to turn the TV on to check the score. I sat in the pew at church, and the minute the pastor said "amen," I was out the door. I didn't want to talk to a single soul. 

So, yeah. All the stuff that used to make me, well, *me*... I just look at all that lately like it belongs to somebody else. It's like I don't even recognize the guy who used to enjoy those things.
Have you felt this low for at least two weeks straight without any significant improvement?

Doc, I swear, we keep circling back to the exact same thing, and I don't know how else to say it to make it stick. I really don't. It's like I'm talking to a brick wall here, no offense. 

Yes. Yes, it has been two weeks straight. Exactly two weeks. Like I told you before, and like I'll tell you again since we're apparently still on this—this whole change in me, this dark cloud, this complete lack of interest in my tomatoes, my woodwork, the Falcons, all of it... it started the exact day my daughter packed up her car and drove out of Georgia for the military. 

That was two weeks ago. Fourteen days. Three hundred and thirty-six hours, if you want to get technical about it. And in all that time, there hasn't been a single day, not a morning, not an afternoon, not a five-minute window where I felt any significant improvement. I haven't felt like myself once. Not once. 

I know you have to ask these things, I get it, I really do. You're just doing your job, checking your boxes, making sure you got the timeline right. I do the same thing at the plant when we're running a safety audit. You gotta be thorough. But I'm telling you, as God is my witness, it has been two solid weeks of this. Ever since she left. No breaks, no letup, no improvement. Just... this. Two weeks straight.
Have you experienced significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life due to these feelings?

Well, doc, that's... yeah, that's exactly why I'm here. I mean, I'm a manager at the plant, right? I'm the guy who usually keeps everything running smooth, making sure everybody's where they need to be, double-checking the safety protocols, keeping the line moving. I've been doing this a long time, and I know that plant like the back of my hand. But lately... man, it's just been a mess. 

I've been making mistakes. Stupid mistakes that I would normally catch in my sleep. Forgetting to sign off on shift reports, mixing up the inventory numbers, just... dropping the ball. And it got bad enough, serious enough, that the other morning, I couldn't even bring myself to walk through the front doors. I just drove into the parking lot, put the truck in park, and sat there. It was still pitch black out, way before dawn, and I just sat in the cab of my truck staring at the steering wheel. Couldn't move. Couldn't make myself go in and face it. That's when one of the supervisors, Dave—good guy, known him for years—he tapped on my window and saw the state I was in. He's the one who got occupational health involved, and that's how I ended up sitting in this chair talking to you. 

And it's not just work, either. It's bleeding into everything. At home, I'm usually the one who handles the finances. I like keeping the books balanced, making sure the mortgage is paid on the first, the electric bill, the water bill, all of it. I got a whole system, a filing cabinet in the den where everything goes. But these last two weeks? The mail just comes through the slot and piles up on the entryway table. I walk right past it. My wife asked me the other day if I paid the insurance premium, and I just looked at her blankly. I hadn't even opened the envelope. I just can't bring myself to care about any of it. The responsibilities are just piling up, and I'm just watching it happen, like I'm paralyzed. So, yes, it's definitely causing some major problems. It's like my whole life is just stalling out.
Have you felt this low for most of every day for at least two weeks straight?

Doc, are you... are you reading off a checklist and just losing your place? Because I swear to you, we just went over this exact same thing not five minutes ago. I feel like we're just spinning our tires in the mud here. 

Like I said before, yes. It has been two weeks. Fourteen days since my daughter left for the military. And when you say "most of every day," well, that's almost putting it too lightly. It's the whole day. From the minute my eyes open at 4:30 in the morning—because I've always been an early riser, you know, usually I like to get up and get a jump on the day, maybe have a quiet cup of coffee before the sun comes up and the neighborhood gets loud—from that very second, it's just heavy. It's sitting right there on my chest. It's there while I'm brushing my teeth, it's there while I'm staring out the window, and it's there all through the afternoon, right up until I lay my head back down on the pillow at night. 

So, yes, most of every day, all of every day, for two solid weeks. I really don't know how many different ways I can explain the timeline to you, doc. I mean, at the plant, if I stood up at the morning briefing and asked my floor guys the same question three times in a row, they'd look at me like I'd lost my marbles. They'd think I finally blew a gasket or something. I know you've probably got a lot of patients and a lot of paperwork on your desk, and maybe they all start blurring together after a while, but I'm giving it to you as straight as I can. Two weeks. Every single day. I just... I don't know what else I can say to make that part clear.
Do you feel like these feelings of sadness and emptiness are interfering with your ability to function in your daily life?

Doc, I... I really gotta ask. Are you feeling alright? Did you not get enough sleep last night? Because I just... I literally just told you all of this. I mean, we just went over this exact same ground not three minutes ago. I feel like I'm stuck in that movie Groundhog Day, just waking up and having the same conversation over and over again. 

But fine. Fine. If you need me to spell it out again for the paperwork, I will. Yes, it is interfering with my daily life. In a big way. Like I just explained, at the plant, I've been making mistakes. Big mistakes. The kind of mistakes a guy with my experience shouldn't be making. And it got so bad, so overwhelming, that I couldn't even make myself walk into the building. I just sat out there in the parking lot in the pitch black, staring at the steering wheel of my truck, completely frozen. If Dave hadn't come along and tapped on the glass, if he hadn't seen the shape I was in and called in occupational health... well, I don't know how long I would've just sat there. That's why I'm here. Because I can't function at work. 

And at home, like I said, it's the same story. I'm usually the guy who keeps the trains running on time. I pay the bills, I balance the checkbook, I make sure everything is squared away in my filing cabinet. But now? The mail just sits there on the table. The bills pile up. My wife asks me about the insurance premium, and I don't even know what to tell her because I haven't even opened the envelope. I just can't bring myself to do it. The responsibilities are just piling up around me, and I'm just watching it happen. So, yes. Yes, it is interfering. It's interfering with absolutely everything. I just... I really hope we can move on to the next question now, doc, because I feel like I'm beating a dead horse here.
Have you experienced little to no pleasure in activities you usually enjoy for at least two weeks straight?

Well, yeah. That’s... I guess that’s a different question, but the answer is still yes. It’s funny you ask it that way, because I was just standing at the kitchen window yesterday—or maybe it was Tuesday, the days are just kind of running together into one long gray stretch right now—and I was looking out at my yard. 

I usually take a lot of pride in my tomato plants. I got these big Beefsteaks I’ve been babying since the spring, you know, tying them up to the stakes, pinching off the suckers, making sure the soil is just right. Usually, I'd be out there every single evening with the hose, just enjoying the quiet and getting my hands dirty. It's peaceful. But now? I look out there and the vines are starting to droop, the bugs are getting to 'em, and I just... I don't care. 

And it ain't just the yard, either. I got a little workbench out in the garage. I like to tinker, do a little woodworking. Nothin' fancy, just sanding down some wood at my bench, making little birdhouses or shelves just to keep my hands busy. The smell of the sawdust, the rhythm of the sandpaper... usually that settles my mind right down after a long week at the plant. But I walked out there the other day to grab a screwdriver, saw my sander and my wood scraps sitting there, and just felt absolutely nothing. It was just a pile of junk to me. Turned right around and went back inside. 

Same thing with Sundays. Usually, I'm the first one parked in his recliner to watch the Falcons play, hollering at the screen, getting all worked up over the play-calling. Or at church, you know? Service ends, and I’m usually the guy hanging around in the vestibule or out in the parking lot for another hour, just staying after church talking, shooting the breeze about the weather or the local news with the other guys. But these last couple weeks since my daughter left? I just slip out the back door as soon as the preacher says 'amen.' I don't want to talk to anybody. I don't want to watch the game. I don't want to touch my tools or my plants. 

I used to mess with my tomato plants, sand wood at my bench, watch the Falcons, and stay after church talking, but lately... I don't know, doc. Lately I just look at all that like it belongs to somebody else. Like I'm just a ghost walking through some other guy's life. It just doesn't mean anything to me right now.
Have your feelings of sadness and emptiness lasted for at least two weeks without any improvement?

Doc... I swear I'm trying to be patient here, I really am. But you're asking me about the two weeks again. I feel like a broken record, and I know I don't have a fancy college degree or nothing, but I know I'm speaking plain English. 

But fine, I'll answer the new part you tacked on there at the end—about the improvement. No. There hasn't been a lick of improvement. Not a single good hour, let alone a good day. This whole change in me has been going on for about two weeks since my daughter left Georgia for the military. And when I say no improvement, I mean it's just been a flat line. 

I keep waiting for it to break, you know? Like a fever. I keep thinking maybe I'll go to sleep, and tomorrow I'll wake up at 4:30 and feel like my old self.
